w: Woodland and open lawns roll down to the Grand Union Canal here, carved out in 1924 from the grounds of the 17th-century Boston Manor House next door. The lake and mature trees are what survive of the wider stately estate once attached to the manor.
s: Canalside remnant of the Boston Manor estate
_facts: Created 1924 from part of the Boston Manor House estate
Adjoins the Grand Union Canal
Combines woodland with open sports space

w: Built in 1909 by architect Nowell Parr on Leighton Road, Northfields, The Forester is Grade II listed and sits on CAMRA's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors -- a shortlist of pubs whose original fittings have survived largely intact.
s: 1909 pub interior on CAMRA's protected list
_facts: Built 1909 by architect Nowell Parr
Grade II listed
On CAMRA's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors

w: Neo-Gothic in imitation of the Decorated style, John Taylor the Younger's church was funded by developer Henry Daniel Davies to serve his new Spring Grove housing estate. Its stone-mullioned nave galleries were built but never used, and the stained glass is by Heaton, Butler and Bayne.
s: Neo-Gothic church built for a Victorian estate
_facts: Designed by John Taylor the Younger
Funded by developer Henry Daniel Davies for the Spring Grove estate
Stained glass by Heaton, Butler and Bayne

w: An 18th-century coaching inn on London Road, altered over the centuries but still Grade II listed. Charles Dickens name-checked it in Oliver Twist, cementing its place as one of Isleworth's oldest surviving pubs.
_facts: Built in the 18th century, with later alterations
Grade II listed
Mentioned by Charles Dickens in Oliver Twist

w: Founded in 1661 by Brian Duppa, Bishop of Winchester, to house ten unmarried women over 50, these almshouses were rebuilt in 1851 in The Vineyard, reusing the original 1661 gateway. Blitz-damaged units were rebuilt again in 1949; residents must still be 65 or over.
s: 1661 almshouses, twice rebuilt, still in use
_facts: Founded 1661 by Brian Duppa, Bishop of Winchester
Rebuilt 1851 in The Vineyard, reusing the 1661 gateway
Blitz-damaged houses rebuilt again in 1949

w: Funded by local donations and built between 1887 and 1889, these twin bridges replaced the ferry that once gave Ferry Road its name. A suspension span crosses the weir stream to a small mid-river island; an iron girder bridge continues on to Ham. Both are Grade II listed.
s: Twin Victorian bridges that replaced a ferry
_facts: Built 1887-1889, funded by local donations
Replaced a ferry that gave Ferry Road its name
Both spans are Grade II listed

w: York House on Richmond Road now serves as the town hall of Richmond upon Thames, having begun life as a stately home near St Mary's Church in central Twickenham. Grade II* listed, its surrounding park carries the same listed status.
s: Twickenham stately home turned town hall
_facts: Grade II* listed former stately home
Now the town hall of Richmond upon Thames
Its surrounding park is separately listed
